title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and two bounds lower and upper, count how many contiguous subarrays have a sum that falls within the inclusive range from lower to upper. Solve it with prefix sums and a merge-sort-based counting technique and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
keyPoints: A subarray sum from index j to i equals prefix[i] minus prefix[j], so the problem reduces to counting prefix-sum pairs whose difference lies in the given range.
Counting qualifying pairs naively is O(n^2), but embedding the count inside a merge sort achieves O(n log n).
During each merge step, two sorted halves allow sliding two pointers over the left half for each right-half prefix to count qualifying pairs in linear time per level.
Use long for prefix sums to avoid integer overflow when subtracting bounds from monetary values.
An alternative approach uses a Fenwick tree over coordinate-compressed prefix values, also achieving O(n log n).
This is a hard-tier problem that fuses prefix sums with order-statistics counting inside a divide-and-conquer framework.

s1_definition.oneliner: Count contiguous subarrays whose sum lies within a given range by reframing the problem as counting prefix-sum pairs and using a merge-sort-based counting technique for O(n log n) time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Prefix-sum reframing** – any subarray sum equals the difference of two prefix sums, so a subarray sum lying in the range [lower, upper] means the left prefix lies in a shifted window relative to the right prefix.
- **Merge-sort counting** – embedding the pair-counting step inside the merge phase of merge sort lets you count qualifying pairs efficiently because both halves are already sorted.
- **Pointer sliding** – for each right-half prefix, two pointers slide over the sorted left half to find the range of qualifying left prefixes, giving linear work per merge level.
- **O(n log n) total** – the log n merge levels each contribute O(n) counting work, plus O(n) merging work.
- **Overflow safety** – prefix sums must use long because subtracting the bounds from accumulated sums can exceed int range on monetary data.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows that can be positive or negative. The compliance team needs to count how many continuous stretches of days had a net total falling between a lower and an upper regulatory threshold, because each such stretch triggers a mandatory disclosure. Rajesh cannot check every pair of days by hand, so he uses prefix sums and a merge-sort counting technique to get the answer in O(n log n) time.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Prefix Sum Reframing
====================

Array:    [-2,  5, -1]
Prefix: [0, -2,  3,  2]

Subarray sum [j..i-1] = P[i] - P[j]

For range [lower, upper]:
  lower <= P[i] - P[j] <= upper
  P[i] - upper <= P[j] <= P[i] - lower


Merge-Sort Counting Flow
=========================

  Prefix array: [0, -2, 3, 2]

  Split:
  ┌───────────┐   ┌───────────┐
  │  [0, -2]  │   │  [3, 2]   │
  └─────┬─────┘   └─────┬─────┘
        │               │
  Split again:    Split again:
  [0] [-2]       [3] [2]
        │               │
  Merge+Count:    Merge+Count:
  [-2, 0]        [2, 3]
  count1          count2
        │               │
        └───────┬───────┘
                │
       Merge + Count across halves:
       Left sorted: [-2, 0]
       Right sorted: [2, 3]

       For each left P[i], slide j1,j2 over right:
       ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
       │  P[i]=-2: window [P[i]-up, P[i]-lo] │
       │  P[i]=0:  window [P[i]-up, P[i]-lo] │
       │  j1,j2 slide forward only ──────►   │
       └──────────────────────────────────┘

       Final sorted: [-2, 0, 2, 3]
       Total count = count1 + count2 + cross_count
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum within an inclusive range [lower, upper], and the efficient solution uses prefix sums combined with a merge-sort-based counting technique. You build prefix sums so that any subarray sum is the difference of two prefixes, and then a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when the left prefix falls in a shifted interval relative to the right prefix. Counting such pairs naively is O(n^2), so you embed the counting inside the merge phase of merge sort.

During each merge step, with the left and right halves already sorted, you slide two pointers over the left half for each prefix in the right half. One pointer advances past values that are too small and the other advances past values that are still in range, and the gap between the pointers is the count of qualifying left endpoints. These pointer scans are linear per merge level, and summed over the log n levels they give O(n log n) total counting work. After counting, you perform the ordinary merge so the array stays sorted for the parent call.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the regulatory reporting team. Daily net cash flows could be positive or negative, and the compliance team needed an exact count of how many continuous stretches had a net total falling within a specific regulatory band, because each such stretch triggered a mandatory disclosure. The prefix-sum plus merge-sort counting computed the answer in O(n log n) time, keeping the nightly regulatory job within its reporting window.

The senior-level insight is that this is a genuine hard-tier problem because it fuses prefix sums with order-statistics counting, and recognizing that the counting can ride along inside a merge sort is the key breakthrough. Always use long prefix sums because subtracting bounds from accumulated monetary values can overflow int. Mentioning the Fenwick tree alternative and the overflow safeguard shows production-grade depth.

Remember one sentence: count of range sum reframes subarray sums as prefix-pair differences and counts qualifying pairs inside a merge sort with sliding pointers for O(n log n) time.
